Chevrolet Virtually Crashed the Silverado 92,000 Times To Make Sure It's Safe
10 photos
Photo: General Motors
Chevrolet conducted roughly 92,000 virtual crash simulations during the development of the redesigned 2027 Chevrolet Silverado 1500 to make sure they are delivering a truck that keeps everyone safe in a wide range of real-world crash scenarios.
GM claims that its engineers were the first in the automotive industry to intentionally crash vehicles to study what happens in the impact, back in the 1930s. Nearly a century later, engineers from General Motors’ Global Safety Product Integration (GSPI) tested thousands of micro-variables, including material thickness and joint welds, occupant body sizes, and seating positions.
For a single 40-mph, 40% frontal overlap crash scenario, the team modeled hundreds of structural and restraint variations before building physical prototypes. The truck carried a 50th-percentile (average) male dummy in the driver's seat and a 5th-percentile (small) female dummy right behind him in the second row.
GM uses a family of approximately 100 full-body crash test dummies, but the number expands to 150 when classified as anthropomorphic test devices. Engineers ran 5,500 airbag tests, taking up to 100 simulations per airbag inside three environmental chambers.
Photo: General Motors Virtual models by no means replaced real-world testing entirely. General Motors still crashed approximately 50 trucks at Building 61 of its Milford Proving Ground in Michigan to verify the computer data and inspect post-crash components.
Technicians strip the interiors down to inspect individual components. They also verify that doors open easily without jamming, fuel lines remain intact, hazard and interior lights turn on, doors automatically unlock, and the OnStar emergency call connects.
Computer simulations accounted for roughly 80% of the pickup truck’s passive safety engineering work and generated nearly 2 petabytes of data, which is basically the equivalent of one trillion pages of documents.
The newly redesigned 2027 Chevrolet Silverado pickup truck features a redesigned frame with boxed sections, new tire deflectors, a collapsing steering column, and a reinforced steel safety cage to manage load paths, including changes required by the presence of an optional panoramic sunroof.
Photo: General Motors To improve rear-seat protection in frontal offset crashes, an area where the 2026 model received only a marginal rating from the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS), GM added rear seatbelt pretensioners and revised the rear seat structure.
By relying heavily on AI-assisted virtual testing instead of sacrificing a large number of expensive physical prototypes right from the get-go, GM can spot weak points and improve design in terms of safety in just weeks rather than months. The auto giant deployed artificial intelligence to debug simulation models, spot structural “hot spots,” and sort through tens of thousands of data points.
The 2027 Chevrolet Silverado Crew Cab entered production this fall, while the Double Cab variant is slated to start rolling off the production line in the second half of 2027. Prices start at $41,395 (destination fee included) for the base Work Truck Regular Cab 2WD with the 2.7-liter TurboMax engine.
